best_field_traits: Perennial in shady moist woods rather than short-lived cool-season weed.
Erect to arching leafy culms often 0.6–1.5 m high, with relatively broad 6–19 mm grass blades.
Open spreading/drooping panicle generally ~10–25 cm long.
Multi-flowered spikelets ~13–30 mm, often with 5–10 florets.
Lemma short straight awn usually ~3–8 mm; surfaces often fine-hairy, but this cannot be confirmed from current photo.
Closed sheaths with soft retrorse hairs, ligule short membranous; botanical treatments differ slightly in typical lengths.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: High-res whole plant with base showing perennial crown
Visible lower closed sheath and hairy node closeup
Glumes, lemmas, and whether mature upper internodes are hairy
crew_field_check: LOOK AT THE SPIKELET, NOT JUST THE DROOP: all four bromes have several florets stacked along one spikelet, often with lemma awns. First decide ANNUAL vs PERENNIAL, then count florets, measure the entire spikelet, individual lemma and awn, and inspect the glume veins and leaf sheath hairs. Nodding inflorescences or long awns alone are not a species ID.
Measure actual mature spikelet(s) with a millimeter ruler.
Inspect lemma/glume or true ligule ONLY where detailed pixels or a collected macro are actually available.
Record uncertain grass to genus, don't force the species from one photo.

comparisons.key_distinctions: Unlike the three other currently installed Bromus cards, B. pubescens is PERENNIAL and often found in shaded moist woodland understory. Japanese brome is a small-spikeleted annual with flexuous panicle branches; B. lanceolatus has unusually long, many-flowered annual spikelets; B. texensis is an annual with shorter awns and requires mature glume/lemma comparison. Habitat or hairiness alone cannot clinch this one.

visual_comparison.memory_rule: Annual japonicus / lanceolatus / texensis versus perennial woodland pubescens. Small loose kinked heads japonicus; giant lance-shaped spikelets lanceolatus; damp shaded perennial pubescens; Texas annual texensis demands short-awn/lemma comparison.
